rewritten_text:
She was right about the rats. Every so often you would see one poke its nose out of a hole in the corner. She said that when she was alone she needed things within reach to throw at them, or they wouldn't leave her in peace. She showed me a lead bar bent into a knot and said she usually had a good aim with it, but she had strained her arm a day or two before and wasn't sure she could still throw straight. She waited for her chance, though, and soon hurled it at a rat. She missed by a long way and cried, ‘Ouch!’ because it hurt her arm so much. Then she told me to try for the next one. I wanted to leave before her husband returned, but naturally I didn't show it. I took the lead and threw it at the first rat that stuck its nose out. If it had stayed there, it would have been a pretty sick rat. She said that was excellent, and she thought I would get the next one. She retrieved the lump of lead and brought it back, along with a skein of yarn she wanted my help with. I held up both hands, and she slipped the skein over them and kept talking about herself and her husband's affairs. But she interrupted herself to say:

‘Watch out for the rats. You'd better keep the lead in your lap, where it's handy.’

Just then she dropped the lump into my lap, and I snapped my legs together to catch it. She went on talking, but only for about a minute. Then she removed the skein, looked straight into my face with a friendly expression, and said:

‘Come on, now, what's your real name?’

‘Wh—what, ma'am?’

‘Your real name. Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob? What is it?’

I think I trembled like a leaf, and I hardly knew what to do. But I said:

‘Please don't make fun of a poor girl like me, ma'am. If I'm in your way here, I'll—’

‘No, you won't. Sit down and stay put. I'm not going to hurt you or tell on you, either. Just trust me and tell me your secret. I'll keep it, and I'll help you besides. My husband will too, if you want. You're an apprentice who's run away, that's all. It's nothing. There's no harm in it. You've been badly treated, and you decided to leave. Bless you, child, I wouldn't tell on you.’

Without me, he would never have been released. Morgan le Fay hated him with all her heart and would never have relented. Yet his crime owed more to carelessness than to deliberate wickedness. He had said her hair was red. Well, it was, but that wasn't the way to describe it. Above a certain social rank, redheads have auburn hair.

Think of it: five of those forty-seven prisoners had been there so long that nobody knew their names, their offenses, or the dates they had been locked up! One woman and four men, all bent and wrinkled, ancient people whose minds had gone dark. They themselves had forgotten those details long ago; at least, they offered only hazy theories, nothing certain and nothing they told the same way twice. Generations of priests had been charged with praying beside the prisoners daily, reminding them that God had placed them there for some wise purpose, and teaching them that He delighted to see people of the lower ranks endure oppression with patience, humility, and submission. These priests had inherited stories about the poor old human wrecks, but nothing else. The stories offered little help, since they concerned only the length of imprisonment, without identifying the offenses. Even with those accounts, all that could be established was that none of the five had seen daylight for thirty-five years. How much longer they had been deprived of it, nobody could guess. The king and queen knew only that these miserable creatures were heirlooms, assets inherited with the throne from the previous management. No history accompanied their transfer, so their new owners considered them worthless and took no interest in them. I asked the queen:

‘Then why on earth didn't you let them go?’

That question baffled her. She couldn't say why she hadn't; the thought had simply never occurred to her. Without realizing it, she was anticipating the actual history of the future prisoners of the Château d'If. I understood now that, given her upbringing, those inherited prisoners were simply possessions, no more and no less. And when we inherit possessions, it doesn't occur to us to throw them away, even if we don't value them.

I brought my procession of human bats into the open air and the dazzling afternoon sunlight, first covering their eyes out of compassion for eyes that light had not tormented in so many years. They were quite a sight. Every one of them was a skeleton, a scarecrow, a goblin, a pitiful horror; the most legitimate offspring imaginable of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church.

Once we had seen our friend properly established in his new office, we turned our thoughts toward Windsor. It was close enough to London that leaving Raymond and Perdita did not feel like a painful separation. We said goodbye at the Protector's Palace. There was something charming in watching my sister enter into the spirit of the performance and try to occupy her position with suitable dignity. Her inward pride and outward modesty conflicted more than ever. Her shyness was genuine: it came from a fear of not being properly valued, and from that same dismissive attitude toward the world's neglect that distinguished Raymond. Perdita, however, thought of other people more consistently than he did. Some of her reserve came from a desire to spare those around her any sense of inferiority, a feeling that never entered her own mind. Her birth and upbringing would have made Idris better suited to ceremonial formalities. Yet the very ease with which habit allowed her to perform them made them tedious to her, whereas Perdita, despite every difficulty, plainly enjoyed her position. Her mind was so full of new ideas that our departure caused her little distress. She said goodbye affectionately and promised to visit soon, but she did not regret the circumstances that separated us. Raymond's high spirits knew no bounds. He scarcely knew what to do with his newly acquired power. His head teemed with plans, although he had settled on none. Still, he promised himself, his friends, and the world that some act of extraordinary glory would distinguish his time as Protector. We talked about them in this way, drawing our reflections, as our reduced party returned to Windsor Castle. We were intensely glad to escape political upheaval and sought our seclusion with renewed pleasure. There was plenty to occupy us, but I now directed my restless energy entirely toward intellectual work. I found concentrated study an excellent remedy for the agitation that idleness would undoubtedly have brought on. Perdita had allowed us to bring Clara back to Windsor, and she and my two beautiful babies supplied endless interest and amusement.

Only Adrian's health troubled our peace. It was visibly deteriorating, although no symptom pointed to a particular illness, unless his increasingly brilliant eyes, animated expression, and flushed cheeks justified our fear of consumption. He himself felt neither pain nor anxiety. He devoted himself eagerly to books, and when he rested from studying, he spent time with the people whose company he loved most: his sister and me.
